name: Nimzo-Indian Defense
summary: The Nimzo-Indian (3...Bb4) pins the knight to fight for the centre with pieces, one of the soundest defences to 1.d4.
intro: The Nimzo-Indian Defense, 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4, pins the c3-knight to contest the e4-square and often saddles White with doubled c-pawns. A hypermodern masterpiece of the strategist Aron Nimzowitsch, it remains a cornerstone of elite repertoires.
line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4

sections.heading: Strategic ideas
paragraphs: The Nimzo-Indian Defense begins with the immediate 3...Bb4, pinning White's knight on c3 against the king. The point is subtle but profound: by tying down the knight, Black fights for control of the central e4-square with pieces rather than committing his own pawns to it. This piece-based struggle for the center is the strategic heart of the opening and a purely hypermodern idea.

Black frequently follows up by exchanging the bishop for the c3-knight, willingly parting with the bishop pair in order to inflict lasting damage on White's structure. In doing so Black poses White a fundamental question about which is worth more: the two bishops and open lines, or a sound, flexible pawn formation. The resulting positions are strategically rich and revolve around exploiting or repairing that imbalance.

sections.heading: Pawn structure
paragraphs: The most characteristic structural feature arises when Black captures on c3 and White recaptures with the b-pawn, leaving White with doubled c-pawns. These doubled pawns can become a long-term weakness, especially the pawn on c4, which Black tries to blockade and attack, often with a knight on a5 and pawns on ...c5 and ...b6. Black may also aim for a light-square blockade to render White's extra bishop passive.

In compensation, White gains the bishop pair and a strong, mobile pawn center. If White can advance the central pawns and open the position, the two bishops sweep across the board and the doubled pawns become a source of central strength rather than weakness. The battle between structure and the bishop pair gives the Nimzo-Indian its distinctive character and makes it a model teaching opening for positional imbalance.

sections.heading: History and background
paragraphs: The Nimzo-Indian is named after Aron Nimzowitsch, the leading theoretician of the hypermodern school, who championed the ideas of controlling the center from a distance, restraint, and prophylaxis. The opening embodies his principles more clearly than perhaps any other, treating the fight for e4 as a matter of piece pressure rather than pawn occupation.

It has long enjoyed a reputation as one of Black's most reliable and respected answers to 1.d4, trusted by positional and dynamic players alike across generations of world-class competition. Because it is both solid and flexible, it appears in the repertoires of players who want a sound but unbalanced game, and it remains a cornerstone of modern opening theory.

keyIdeas: The bishop move ...Bb4 pins the c3-knight and fights for e4 with pieces instead of pawns
Black often trades ...Bxc3, giving up the bishop pair to damage White's pawns
White's recapture bxc3 creates doubled c-pawns that can become a durable weakness
The central strategic imbalance is White's bishop pair versus Black's superior structure
Black blockades and pressures the c4-pawn, frequently with ...c5, ...b6 and a knight on a5
White seeks to open the position so the two bishops and mobile center come alive

white: Recapture on c3 with the b-pawn and use the bishop pair with a broad pawn center
Prepare the e4 advance, sometimes with f3 and Ne2, to seize central space
Open the position so the two bishops gain scope across long diagonals
In lines that avoid doubled pawns, aim for harmonious development and a spatial edge
Neutralize Black's pressure on c4 and turn the doubled pawns into central strength
black: Play ...Bxc3 at the right moment to saddle White with doubled c-pawns
Blockade and attack the c4-pawn with ...c5, ...b6, ...Ba6 and a knight on a5
Restrain White's e4 break by keeping pieces trained on the square, for example ...d5 and ...Nf6
Exploit the light squares if White's light-squared bishop becomes passive
Keep the structure sound so the long-term pawn imbalance favors the endgame
